body_html:
Mexican slang is everywhere in the Spanish you hear in the United States: on TikTok, in Mexican movies, in family group chats and in conversations with coworkers from Jalisco or Mexico City. Words like güey, chido, neta and no manches appear in almost every casual conversation, yet most textbooks never mention them. After years of translating Mexican Spanish, here are the words I hear most, what they really mean, how strong they are and which ones you should only use with close friends.

Quick answer
  • Friendly and safe: ¿Qué onda?, chido, padre, órale, ¿neta?
  • Very common but casual: güey, no manches, chamba, lana
  • Use with care: naco is insulting; anything with pedo or madre can be vulgar.
  • Mexicans adjust slang to the situation, so follow their lead.
{{toc}}

Mexican slang greetings and reactions

WordMeaningExample
¿Qué onda?What’s up?¿Qué onda, güey? ¿Cómo estás? (Hey dude, how are you?)
¿Qué pex?What’s up? (very casual)¿Qué pex, carnal? (What’s up, bro?)
ÓraleOkay! / Wow! / Come on!¡Órale, vamos! (Okay, let’s go!)
¿Neta?Really? / Seriously?¿Neta te casas? (You’re really getting married?)
No manchesNo way! / You’re kidding!¡No manches, qué caro! (No way, that’s so expensive!)
HíjoleOh no / YikesHíjole, se me olvidó. (Oh no, I forgot.)
AguasWatch out!¡Aguas con el perro! (Watch out for the dog!)
¿Mande?Sorry? / Pardon?—¡Juan! —¿Mande? (“Juan!” “Yes?”)

¿Mande? deserves a special mention. It is the polite Mexican way to answer when someone calls you or when you didn’t hear, and children are taught to use it instead of ¿qué?. Using it will make you sound well brought up.

Describing things: chido, padre, chafa

WordMeaningExample
chidocool, greatTu carro está bien chido. (Your car is really cool.)
padrecool, great¡Qué padre! (How cool!)
chafacheap, poor qualityEste celular está bien chafa. (This phone is really cheap.)
gachobad, mean, unfairQué gacho lo que te hizo. (What he did to you was really mean.)
fresaposh, preppyEs muy fresa. (She’s very preppy.)
cañóntough, difficultEstá cañón el examen. (The exam is really tough.)

Bien is often used as an intensifier in Mexico, so bien chido means “really cool” and bien caro means “really expensive”.

{{image:2}}

People, work and money

WordMeaningExample
güey / weydude, guyEse güey es mi primo. (That guy is my cousin.)
cuatebuddy, friendEs mi cuate de la prepa. (He’s my buddy from high school.)
carnalbrother, close friend¿Qué onda, carnal? (What’s up, bro?)
morro / morrayoung guy / young womanEsa morra es mi hermana. (That girl is my sister.)
chamacokidLos chamacos están jugando. (The kids are playing.)
chambajob, workTengo mucha chamba. (I have a lot of work.)
lanamoneyNo traigo lana. (I don’t have any money on me.)
chelabeer¿Vamos por unas chelas? (Shall we go for some beers?)
crudahangoverTengo una cruda horrible. (I have a terrible hangover.)

Güey is the most famous Mexican slang word. Between friends it is affectionate and used constantly, almost like punctuation. With strangers, older people or at work, it can sound disrespectful, so wait until you hear people use it with you.

Ahorita, ahorita and the Mexican sense of time

Ahorita literally means “right now”, but in Mexico it can mean anything from “in a second” to “later” to “probably never”. Ahorita vengo could mean five minutes or an hour. To ask for real urgency, people say ahorita mismo or ya.

This is a good example of why slang is cultural, not just vocabulary. Knowing the word is half the job; knowing how people use it is the other half. I write more about these regional differences in {{link:latin-american-vs-spain-spanish|Latin American vs Spain Spanish}}.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Words to use with care

Some very common Mexican words are vulgar or insulting. You will hear them constantly in movies and among friends, but as a learner it is better to recognize them than to use them:

  • naco: a classist insult meaning tacky or low class. Avoid it.
  • ¿Qué pedo?: “What’s up?” among close friends, but pedo literally means fart and is vulgar. ¿Qué pex? is a softer version.
  • madre: expressions with madre range from positive (a toda madre, awesome) to very offensive. Context and tone matter enormously.
  • chingar and its many forms: the most versatile and most vulgar verb in Mexican Spanish. Recognize it; don’t use it.

The Asociación de Academias de la Lengua Española documents many of these words, with their regional meaning, in its Diccionario de americanismos.

A sample chat between friends

Dani: ¿Qué onda, güey? ¿Vamos por unos tacos?
What’s up, dude? Want to go get some tacos?

Luis: Órale, pero ahorita no puedo, tengo mucha chamba.
Sure, but I can’t right now, I have a lot of work.

Dani: ¿Neta? Ya son las nueve.
Seriously? It’s already nine.

Luis: Sí, está cañón. ¿Mañana?
Yeah, it’s rough. Tomorrow?

Dani: Va. Pero tú invitas, que yo no traigo lana.
Deal. But you’re paying, I don’t have any money.

Va is a very common Mexican way to say “okay” or “deal”. For more texting style and abbreviations, see {{link:texting-in-spanish|texting in Spanish}}.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes with Mexican slang

  • Using güey with your partner’s parents. Save it for friends your own age.
  • Using slang in formal writing. Emails and job interviews call for standard Spanish; see {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}}.
  • Taking ahorita literally. Ask ¿ahorita ahorita? if you really need to know.
  • Using Mexican slang in Spain or Argentina. Many words don’t travel. Compare {{link:spain-slang|Spain slang}} and {{link:argentine-slang|Argentine slang}}.
{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Mexican slang is the fastest way to understand real conversations, from TikTok to family dinners. Start with the friendly words, listen for how people use the casual ones, and leave the vulgar ones for recognition only. For slang from other countries, see my guide to {{link:spanish-slang|Spanish slang}}.

faq.q: What is the most common Mexican slang word?
faq.a: Probably güey (dude), followed by qué onda, chido, neta and no manches.
Among friends it is affectionate and very common. With strangers, older people or at work, it can sound disrespectful.
Literally “right now”, but in practice anything from “in a minute” to “later”.
A few friendly words like qué onda, chido and órale are safe. Avoid vulgar words until you understand them well.
